pages.cardBlurb: What the 2022 amendment changed — casual workers brought inside the duty — and what employers must actually do.
pages.h1: The PPE at Work Regulations, updated for 2022.
pages.metaTitle: PPE at Work Regulations 2022 Explained | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: What the PPE at Work (Amendment) Regulations 2022 changed — extending employer PPE duties to casual 'limb (b)' workers — and the practical checklist of what employers must do.
pages.lede: The 2022 amendment to the PPE at Work Regulations made one change with wide ripples: the duty to provide protective equipment no longer stops at employees. If your workforce includes casual or gig-style workers, the rules very likely now include them.

blocks.h2: One word — workers — did the work
blocks.html:
The original 1992 regulations placed PPE duties on employers toward their employees. The 2022 amendment extended those same duties to "limb (b)" workers — people with casual, irregular or gig-style arrangements who work under a contract personally and aren't running their own business. Zero-hours bar staff, casual warehouse labour, some couriers: if the risk assessment says the job needs PPE, they're now owed it on the same terms as employees.

The duties themselves didn't change, they just cover more people: assess the risk, provide suitable PPE free of charge where the risk requires it, maintain and replace it, store it properly, train workers in its use — and workers must use it as trained.

Include casual workers

blocks.html: This page is a plain-English summary, not legal advice. The regulations, HSE guidance and your sector's specifics govern — and rules evolve. For anything contentious (worker status especially), check HSE's current guidance or take advice. What this page can promise: if the duty applies, the kit side is straightforward — certified stock, sized to the wearer, replaced when worn.

faq.q: What did the PPE at Work (Amendment) Regulations 2022 change?
faq.a: They extended employers' PPE duties beyond employees to 'limb (b)' workers — casual and gig-style workers under a personal work contract. Where a risk assessment requires PPE, those workers must now receive it free, maintained and with training, on the same basis as employees.

faq.q: Can an employer charge for PPE?
faq.a: No — PPE required by the risk assessment must be provided free of charge, and that includes replacements when kit wears out. Charging, deposits or wage deductions for required PPE aren't permitted.

faq.q: Who counts as a limb (b) worker?
faq.a: Broadly: someone who contracts to do work personally, isn't an employee, but also isn't genuinely running their own business toward your organisation as a client. Status questions can be genuinely tricky — where it matters, check HSE guidance or take advice rather than guessing.

pages.cardBlurb: The clean split: required PPE is always the employer's cost; uniform is a policy question — with rules around the edges.
pages.metaTitle: Who Pays for Workwear & PPE? The Rules | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: The employer/employee split on paying for work clothing — required PPE is always employer-funded, uniform is contractual, and wage deductions have a minimum-wage floor.
pages.lede: One question, two very different answers depending on what the garment is. Protective equipment the job requires: the employer pays, no exceptions. Branded uniform and everyday workwear: a policy question — with legal guard-rails people forget.

blocks.h2: First sort the garment into its legal box
blocks.html:
PPE — anything the risk assessment requires for protection: safety boots, hi-vis, gloves, FR kit, eye protection. The law is blunt: the employer provides it free, maintains it and replaces it (the 2022 rules). "We'll deduct the boots from your first wage" is not a lawful policy for required PPE.

Uniform and ordinary workwear — branded polos, smart trousers, the non-protective wardrobe: no general legal duty to fund it. Most employers do (it's their brand on the chest), some operate purchase or contribution schemes, and the contract or policy sets the terms. The edges are where trouble lives: required purchases and deductions must not take pay below the National Minimum Wage in the relevant pay period — a rule that has caught major employers with "buy black shoes" dress codes — and deductions from wages need a contractual basis or written consent.

blocks.html: Summary, not legal advice — employment contracts, sector agreements and current HMRC/HSE/ACAS guidance govern the specifics, and edge cases (agency staff, deposits, leaver deductions) genuinely vary. The safe defaults: never charge for required PPE, put uniform terms in writing, and keep any worker cost above the minimum-wage floor.

faq.q: Can my employer make me pay for safety boots?
faq.a: Not if the job requires them — PPE identified by the risk assessment must be provided free, including replacements. Employers can offer optional upgrades workers pay toward, but a free compliant option must always exist.

faq.q: Do employers have to pay for uniforms?
faq.a: There's no general legal duty to fund non-protective uniform — the contract or policy decides, and most employers fund branded kit. The guard-rail: required clothing costs or deductions must not take pay below the National Minimum Wage in the pay period.

faq.q: Can an employer deduct uniform costs from wages?
faq.a: Only with a contractual basis or prior written agreement, and never below the minimum-wage floor for required items. Deductions for lost or damaged kit are policy territory that needs the same footing — and required PPE can't be charged for at all.

pages.cardBlurb: The modest-but-real HMRC allowance for washing your own uniform — who qualifies, what it's worth, how to claim free.
pages.h1: Uniform tax relief: small, real, and free to claim.
pages.metaTitle: Uniform Tax Relief Explained: Who Can Claim | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: HMRC's flat-rate allowance for maintaining a recognisable uniform or protective clothing at your own expense — who qualifies, roughly what it's worth, and how to claim without paying an agent.
pages.lede: If you wash, repair or replace a recognisable uniform or protective clothing at your own expense, HMRC operates a flat-rate tax allowance for it. It's modest money — but it's real, backdateable, and free to claim directly. Never pay a claims firm a cut of it.

blocks.html:
The employee version of the relief works when three things line up: you wear a recognisable uniform or protective clothing for work (branded kit, hi-vis, chef whites, scrubs — not ordinary clothes you also wear to work); your employer requires it; and you bear the maintenance cost yourself — washing at home rather than employer-laundered. Miss any leg (employer launders it, or the "uniform" is just a dress code) and the claim fails.

The mechanics: HMRC publishes flat-rate expenses by occupation — a standard rate for most uniformed workers, with higher rates for listed trades — and the relief is that allowance times your tax rate, adjusted through your tax code. It's tens of pounds a year, not hundreds: worth claiming, not worth paying anyone to claim.

blocks.h2: Claiming it, in four short steps
head: Step
What happens
rows: Check the flat rate for your job

Backdate

blocks.html: Two warnings that save money. First: rates and rules are HMRC's and change — check the current figures on gov.uk before relying on any number, including ours. Second: an industry of claims firms exists to file this trivially simple claim for 25–40% of your refund — some aggressively. The claim is free, short and designed for ordinary people; keep the whole refund.

Self-employed workers deduct genuinely protective clothing and true uniform as business expenses through their accounts instead — the flat-rate employee route above isn't theirs, but the principle (protective and branded kit is claimable; everyday clothing isn't) carries over.

What never qualifies: ordinary clothes worn for work (the classic dark-suit case), kit your employer launders, and PPE — because required PPE must be employer-funded in the first place, there should be no worker cost to relieve.

faq.q: Can I claim tax relief for washing my work uniform?
faq.a: If you wear a recognisable uniform or protective clothing your employer requires, and you maintain it at your own expense, generally yes — via HMRC's flat-rate expense allowance, claimed directly and typically backdateable four tax years. Check current rates and rules on gov.uk.

faq.q: How much is uniform tax relief worth?
faq.a: Modest money: the relief is the flat-rate allowance for your occupation multiplied by your tax rate — tens of pounds a year for most people, more for some listed trades. Real enough to claim in five minutes; never worth paying a claims firm a percentage of.

faq.q: Does a dress code count as a uniform for tax relief?
faq.a: No — 'wear smart black clothes' doesn't qualify, because the clothing isn't a recognisable uniform. Branded kit, protective clothing, and clearly uniform garments (whites, scrubs, hi-vis) are what the relief covers, and only when you bear the upkeep cost.

pages.cardTitle: UKCA vs CE marking on PPE, explained
pages.cardBlurb: Two marks, one meaning — what changed after Brexit, what's accepted where, and what a buyer actually needs to check.
pages.h1: UKCA vs CE: what the mark on your PPE means.
pages.metaTitle: UKCA vs CE Marking on PPE & Workwear Explained | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: UKCA and CE marking on PPE decoded — what each mark certifies, what Great Britain and Northern Ireland accept, why both marks appear on one product, and what buyers should actually verify.
pages.lede: Since Brexit, UK-sold PPE can carry a CE mark, a UKCA mark, or both — and buyers regularly worry they've bought the wrong one. The honest news: for almost all workwear and PPE, the two marks certify conformity with what are essentially the same technical standards, and the practical checks are about documents, not logos.

blocks.html:
PPE sold in the EU conforms to Regulation (EU) 2016/425 and carries a CE mark. After Brexit, Great Britain adopted the same regulation into domestic law with a British mark — UKCA — and its own list of designated standards, which for PPE mirror the EU's harmonised ones. In practice the certified performance of a garment is identical either way: an EN ISO 20471 hi-vis jacket is the same jacket under either mark.

What's accepted where: the UK government has repeatedly extended recognition of CE marking for most goods sold in Great Britain — including PPE — so CE-marked kit remains lawful to place on the GB market, and much stock sensibly carries both marks. Northern Ireland follows EU rules, so CE (alone or alongside UKCA) is the operative mark there. Because deadlines in this area have moved several times, treat current government guidance as the authority on dates.

blocks.html: Summary, not legal advice. Conformity-marking transition dates have been extended more than once; for placing products on the market or import decisions, check current GOV.UK guidance rather than relying on any dated article — this one included.

faq.q: Is CE-marked PPE still legal in the UK?
faq.a: For Great Britain, yes — the government has extended recognition of CE marking for most goods including PPE, so CE-marked kit can lawfully be sold and used, and much of the market carries CE and UKCA together. Northern Ireland follows EU rules, where CE is the operative mark. Check current GOV.UK guidance for dates, which have moved several times.

faq.q: Is UKCA better than CE?
faq.a: No — they certify conformity with essentially the same technical standards. A garment's protection is defined by the standard and class on its label (say, EN ISO 20471 Class 3), not by which conformity logo sits next to it. Many products carry both marks to serve both markets.

faq.q: What paperwork should PPE come with?
faq.a: A Declaration of Conformity naming the applicable standards and the notified/approved body, plus user information. For Category III PPE — FR clothing, chemical suits, fall protection — certification includes ongoing production surveillance. A supplier who can't produce the DoC is telling you something.

pages.cardBlurb: There's no 'hi-vis law' — there's a risk-assessment duty that usually concludes hi-vis. How the logic actually runs.
pages.h1: When hi-vis is required: the actual legal logic.
pages.metaTitle: When Is Hi-Vis Required By Law? UK Rules Explained | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: Is hi-vis a legal requirement? The UK logic explained — the PPE regulations' risk-assessment duty, where hi-vis becomes effectively mandatory (roads, rail, sites, vehicles), and who decides the class.
pages.lede: Search for 'hi-vis law UK' and you won't find an act that says 'wear yellow'. What exists is stronger: a duty to assess risks and provide the PPE the assessment demands — and around moving vehicles, that assessment reaches hi-vis so reliably that the duty and the garment have fused in practice.

heroMeta.l: The trigger in almost every case
Required PPE is the employer's cost

blocks.html:
The chain runs: the PPE at Work Regulations require employers to assess risks and provide suitable PPE free where risks can't be controlled otherwise → being struck by a moving vehicle is a classic residual risk → high-visibility clothing (EN ISO 20471) is the recognised control → so wherever people and vehicles share space, the assessment lands on hi-vis and it becomes, in effect, mandatory. That's why the same conclusion appears on construction sites, in warehouse traffic routes, at loading bays, on airport aprons and roadside verges — not because a statute names each place, but because the assessment does the same maths everywhere.

Some environments harden it further: rail has its own binding standard (orange, RIS-3279-TOM), road and highways work follows sector codes that specify class by road speed (the class logic), and sites simply write hi-vis into their entry rules — at which point refusing it is a site-access issue, not a debate. The employer picks the class through the assessment; the employee's duty is to wear what's provided.

Practical position
rows: Construction sites
Effectively universal via site rules — Class 2 minimum is the norm
Roads & highways
Sector codes specify class by speed — Class 3 on high-speed roads
Rail infrastructure

Required on traffic routes per the site's traffic plan

blocks.html: Summary, not legal advice. Duties turn on specific circumstances and current guidance — for decisions with legal consequences, check HSE/GOV.UK guidance or take advice.

faq.q: Is there a law that says you must wear hi-vis?
faq.a: Not by name — the legal duty comes from the PPE at Work Regulations: assess risks, provide suitable PPE free of charge where risks remain. Around moving vehicles that assessment reliably concludes hi-vis, and site rules and sector codes (roads, rail) then make it explicit and enforceable in practice.

faq.q: Can my employer make me wear hi-vis?
faq.a: Yes — where the risk assessment requires it, wearing provided PPE is part of the employee's own legal duty, and sites can make it a condition of entry. The employer's side of the bargain is providing suitable, properly fitting hi-vis at no cost.

faq.q: Who decides between Class 2 and Class 3?
faq.a: The employer's risk assessment, steered by sector codes: higher vehicle speeds, poorer light and less separation push toward Class 3; controlled, low-speed environments sit at Class 2. Rail is separate — orange to the rail standard, regardless of class arguments.

pages.cardTitle: Are safety boots a legal requirement?
pages.cardBlurb: The risk-assessment duty, who pays, whether sites can insist — the footwear questions answered straight.
pages.h1: Safety boots and the law, answered straight.
pages.metaTitle: Are Safety Boots A Legal Requirement UK? | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: Are safety boots legally required? The UK position — the risk-assessment duty, employer payment obligations, site entry rules, self-employed workers and what happens when employees refuse.
pages.lede: Like hi-vis, safety footwear has no act of parliament to its name — and the same stronger thing instead: where a risk assessment finds foot hazards (dropped loads, punctures, crush), suitable safety footwear becomes required PPE that the employer provides free. From there, the practical questions are about edges.

heroMeta.l: Can exceed the law, and do

blocks.html:
The core position: where risks to feet can't be eliminated — falling materials, punctures underfoot, crush from wheels and plant — the PPE regulations make suitable safety footwear (EN ISO 20345) required PPE, provided and paid for by the employer. The who-pays rules are blunt: charging workers for required PPE, or docking it from wages, isn't lawful.

The edges people actually ask about: Sites can — and do — require safety boots for entry even where a task-level argument might not, because a blanket rule is easier to run than a per-visitor assessment; that's contract and access, and it's binding in practice. Refusal: an employee who won't wear provided safety footwear is breaching their own statutory duty, and employers can treat it as a disciplinary matter — the well-worn tribunal ground is that safety rules survive comfort objections where the risk is real (medical issues are handled through alternatives like orthopaedic-compatible footwear, not exemption by default). Office visitors walking a marked route generally don't need boots; step onto the floor proper and the site rule applies. The 2022 label changes (S1PS/S1PL and friends) changed codes, not duties.

Short answer
rows: Can I be charged for required boots?
No — required PPE is free, deposits and deductions included
Can a site insist even for a short visit?
Yes — entry conditions can exceed the legal minimum
Can I wear my own boots?

What if boots hurt?

Self-employed?

blocks.html: Summary, not legal advice. Duties turn on specific circumstances and current guidance — for decisions with legal consequences, check HSE/GOV.UK guidance or take advice.

faq.q: Do employers have to provide safety boots?
faq.a: Where the risk assessment identifies foot hazards requiring PPE, yes — suitable safety footwear provided free of charge, replaced when worn out. That covers most construction, warehouse, manufacturing and yard roles. The employer can specify exactly which spec (S1P, S3 and so on) the assessment demands.

faq.q: Can I refuse to wear safety boots at work?
faq.a: Not usefully — employees have their own legal duty to use provided PPE, and refusal where the risk is real is a disciplinary matter that tribunals have consistently upheld. Genuine fit or medical problems are addressed through alternative compliant footwear, which employers should engage with.

faq.q: Do visitors to sites need safety boots?
faq.a: On most sites, yes beyond reception or marked walkways — blanket entry rules are standard because per-visitor assessment isn't practical. Many sites keep visitor boots; regular visitors are better served owning a pair that fits.

pages.cardBlurb: Under-18s on site — the stronger risk-assessment duty, the tasks that stay off-limits, and kit in sizes that actually fit.
pages.h1: Young workers: the duty gets stronger, not smaller.
pages.metaTitle: PPE For Young Workers & Apprentices: The Rules | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: PPE and under-18s at work — the enhanced risk-assessment duty for young workers, restricted tasks, why adult-sized PPE fails teenagers, and the employer checklist for apprentice intake.
pages.lede: A 17-year-old apprentice triggers duties a 27-year-old doesn't: the law treats young workers' inexperience, developing bodies and unfamiliarity with risk as factors the employer must specifically assess. PPE is where that duty gets physical — because kit sized and specced for adults quietly fails smaller, younger wearers.

blocks.h2: What changes when the worker is young
blocks.html:
Employers must make a specific risk assessment before a young person starts, accounting for inexperience, immaturity and lack of hazard awareness — and for the youngest (under school-leaving age or on work experience) that assessment is shared with parents. Certain exposures are restricted for under-18s outright or pending training and supervision: the well-known examples cluster around high-risk machinery, some chemical exposures and heavy vibration, and trades' own schemes (chainsaw certification being the classic) gate tasks behind age and competence regardless of enthusiasm.

PPE's role in this is mostly about fit and supervision. Adult-default kit fails young workers in predictable ways: gloves a size too big wreck grip, hi-vis drapes, boots on the wrong last cause the blisters that end up in trainers — the same physics as our women's-fit guide, applied to smaller frames generally. Buy the small end of ranges properly (the apprentice kit list covers the personal side), induct the wearer in why each item exists, and use the site's flag systems — the blue hat exists precisely so the whole site helps supervise.

rows: Specific risk assessment

blocks.html: Summary, not legal advice. Duties turn on specific circumstances and current guidance — for decisions with legal consequences, check HSE/GOV.UK guidance or take advice.

faq.q: Do apprentices need a separate risk assessment?
faq.a: Employers must specifically assess risks to young workers before they start, taking account of inexperience and immaturity — for under-school-leaving-age placements, findings are shared with parents. It's an enhanced duty on top of the general assessment, not a repeat of it.

faq.q: What jobs can't under-18s do?
faq.a: Work beyond their physical or psychological capacity, and certain high-risk exposures — dangerous machinery, some chemical and vibration exposures — unless it's necessary training under competent supervision with risks reduced. Trade schemes add their own age and competence gates; the assessment documents the specifics.

faq.q: Does PPE for young workers differ from adult PPE?
faq.a: Same standards, different priority on fit: young and smaller-framed workers need the small end of glove, boot and garment ranges ordered deliberately — oversized PPE degrades protection. Pair it with induction that explains each item's purpose; understanding is what keeps kit worn unsupervised.

pages.cardBlurb: Deposits, deductions and 'buy your own' policies — where the line sits between lawful uniform rules and unlawful charging.
pages.h1: Uniform costs: what can come out of wages.
pages.metaTitle: Uniform Deductions From Wages: UK Rules Explained | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: Can employers charge for uniforms or deduct from wages? The UK rules — PPE must be free, uniform deductions need written agreement and can't breach minimum wage, deposits and leaver clawbacks explained.
pages.lede: Between 'required PPE is free' and 'you must wear black trousers you bought yourself' lies a strip of genuinely confusing territory: deposits, leaver deductions, branded kit charges. The rules that govern it are worth knowing on both sides of the payslip — and minimum wage is where careless policies actually break the law.

blocks.html:
Layer one — PPE: anything required by the risk assessment is provided free, full stop — no purchase, no deposit, no leaver clawback for the hi-vis. That's the who-pays rule and it has no exceptions worth planning around.

Layer two — uniform proper: employers can operate charges around non-PPE uniform (deposits against return, deductions for unreturned kit on leaving) but only through the wage-deduction rules: agreed in writing before the event, and reasonable in scale. Blanket 'we'll dock your last week' habits without signed agreement are unlawful deductions, recoverable at tribunal.

Layer three — the minimum-wage trap: money workers must spend on uniform (buying specified black trousers, paying a deposit, laundering charges) counts against their pay for minimum-wage purposes in the pay period it happens. A minimum-wage worker required to buy £40 of specified clothing has been paid below the floor that week — this is the mistake that puts household-name employers on HMRC's naming lists. The clean answers: provide the kit, or pay an allowance that covers it — and remember employees required to launder distinctive uniform at their own cost may claim tax relief back the other way.

blocks.html: Summary, not legal advice. Duties turn on specific circumstances and current guidance — for decisions with legal consequences, check HSE/GOV.UK guidance or take advice.

faq.q: Can my employer make me pay for my uniform?
faq.a: For required PPE, never. For ordinary uniform, an employer can require specific clothing or operate deposit/deduction schemes only with prior written agreement — and any cost the worker bears counts against minimum wage in that pay period, which is where many policies quietly become unlawful.

faq.q: Can uniform costs be deducted from a final payslip?
faq.a: Only if a deduction for unreturned or damaged kit was agreed in writing beforehand (in the contract or a signed agreement) and the amount is reasonable. Without that prior agreement it's an unlawful deduction from wages, recoverable through tribunal.

faq.q: Do uniform costs affect minimum wage?
faq.a: Yes — money a worker must spend to comply with uniform requirements (buying specified items, deposits, laundering charges) reduces their pay for NMW calculation purposes in that period. Employers at or near the wage floor should provide uniform rather than require purchases.

pages.cardBlurb: Which kit needs formal inspection, which needs pre-use checks, and the paperwork that proves either happened.
pages.h1: PPE inspections: checks, records and who signs.
pages.metaTitle: PPE Inspection & Records: What The Rules Require | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: PPE inspection duties explained — pre-use checks vs formal recorded inspections, which equipment needs which (fall arrest, RPE, helmets, everyday kit), retention of records and replacement triggers.
pages.lede: Providing PPE is half the duty; the other half is keeping it working — maintained, checked, replaced. The rules scale sensibly: a glove gets a glance, a harness gets a signed record. Knowing which regime each item sits in is what keeps both the workforce and the paperwork defensible.

heroMeta.l: Fall arrest and RPE leave paper trails
Everyday kit retires on state, not date

blocks.h2: A glance, a check, a record
blocks.html:
Everything gets pre-use checks: the wearer's quick look — tears, contamination, expired date stamps, seized fittings. It's informal, it's every use, and inductions should teach what 'failed' looks like per item (our care pages — hi-vis condition, FR retirement signs, repair-or-replace logic — are effectively the syllabus).

Some kit adds formal, recorded inspection by a competent person: fall-arrest equipment leads the list (periodic detailed inspections, at least annually and usually more often, recorded per item with unique IDs), followed by RPE — reusable respirators need documented monthly-style examinations plus fit-test records per wearer — and inspection-and-test regimes attach to insulating gloves for electrical work and similar Category III equipment. Helmets sit between: no statutory inspection interval, but date-of-manufacture stamps, maker's service life and post-impact replacement make an informal register worthwhile on any site that issues them (the age checker does the date maths).

The records themselves: what was inspected (unique ID), when, by whom, findings, next due. Keep them at least through the equipment's life; they're the first thing asked for after an incident — and their absence reads as an unmanaged system regardless of the kit's actual state.

blocks.html: Summary, not legal advice. Duties turn on specific circumstances and current guidance — for decisions with legal consequences, check HSE/GOV.UK guidance or take advice.

faq.q: What PPE needs formal inspection?
faq.a: Fall-arrest equipment heads the list — periodic detailed inspection by a competent person, recorded per item — followed by reusable RPE (documented examinations plus fit-test records) and specialist items like electrical insulating gloves. Everyday PPE runs on pre-use checks and condition-based replacement instead.

faq.q: How long should PPE inspection records be kept?
faq.a: At least through the equipment's service life, and organisations commonly keep them longer — they're primary evidence after any incident. Each record should identify the item uniquely, the inspector, the date, findings and the next inspection due.

faq.q: Do hard hats need inspection records?
faq.a: No statutory interval exists, but helmets carry date-of-manufacture stamps and manufacturers state service lives — so a simple issue register with dates, plus replace-on-impact discipline, is cheap defensibility. The pre-use glance for cracks and UV chalking does the daily work.

pages.h1: Fit testing: what the mask rating assumes.
pages.metaTitle: Face Fit Testing Explained: FFP Masks & The Rules | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: Face-fit testing decoded — why UK guidance requires it for tight-fitting RPE, qualitative vs quantitative methods, when to re-test, the clean-shaven rule and what a pass does and doesn't prove.
pages.lede: Every FFP rating assumes something the box never mentions: that the mask seals to this particular face. Fit testing is how that assumption gets verified per person — it's embedded in UK health-and-safety expectations for tight-fitting RPE at work, it takes twenty minutes, and skipping it converts certified protection into guesswork.

blocks.html:
Qualitative testing covers disposables and half-masks: the wearer performs exercises under a hood while a bitter or sweet aerosol is sprayed — taste it and the seal failed. Cheap, portable, pass/fail. Quantitative testing counts particles inside and outside the mask (or measures pressure) to produce a numeric fit factor — required for full-face masks and available for anything tight-fitting. Both test a specific mask model and size on a specific face: pass on one model and the result transfers to nothing else — which is why fit-tested workplaces standardise mask models, and why the test record names the exact product.

When it happens: before first use of tight-fitting RPE, and again when the mask model changes or the face does — significant weight change, dental work, scarring. And the rule it enforces daily: clean-shaven where the seal sits, every shift, because the test that passed a smooth face says nothing about Friday's stubble. Beards move wearers to loose-fitting powered hoods (the RPE ladder), not to hopeful FFP3s. What a pass proves is narrow and valuable: this mask can seal to this face — worn properly, with the discipline the rating maths assumes.

head: Question
Answer
rows: Who needs it?
Every wearer of tight-fitting RPE at work — disposable or reusable
Which method?
Qualitative suffices for FFPs and half-masks; quantitative for full-face
How often?
Before first use; repeat on mask change or facial change — periodic re-tests are good practice
Who tests?
A competent tester — accreditation schemes exist and are the safe hire
The record
Names wearer, mask model and size, method, result, date

blocks.html: Summary, not legal advice. Duties turn on specific circumstances and current guidance — for decisions with legal consequences, check HSE/GOV.UK guidance or take advice.

faq.q: Is face-fit testing a legal requirement?
faq.a: UK guidance under COSHH and related regulations makes fit testing the expected demonstration that tight-fitting RPE is suitable — in practice, inspectors treat unfit-tested tight-fitting RPE as a compliance failure. It applies to disposable FFPs just as much as reusable masks.

faq.q: How is a face-fit test done?
faq.a: Qualitatively: exercises under a hood with a bitter/sweet test aerosol — tasting it means the seal leaks. Quantitatively: instruments count particles inside vs outside the mask for a numeric fit factor. Either way the result applies only to the exact mask model and size tested on that face.

faq.q: Does a fit test work with a beard?
faq.a: No — the test enforces what the physics requires: skin contact where the seal sits. Stubble in the seal line fails tests and defeats passed ones. Wearers who keep facial hair use loose-fitting powered RPE (hoods) instead of tight-fitting masks.
